summary: Defines a protocol that lets a device ask a server in its local access network where it is. The request and response travel over HTTP or HTTP over TLS, and the answer can be location information itself or a reference to it. It is designed to be extensible and independent of the way the network is built.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD) lets a device ask a Location Information Server in its access network for location information. The server can return the location itself or a URI that refers to it; because location is sensitive, the RFC describes safeguards for identifying the server and protecting the response.

questions: how does a device ask the network for its location
how does a device get its location from the network
what is a location information server
subtitle: Lets a device request its location from a server in its access network.

tldr.problem: A device may not be able to determine its own location, or may need location information from the network it is connected to.
tldr.mechanism: HELD defines XML requests to a Location Information Server for location data directly or for a URI that refers to the data, and describes HTTP and HTTPS transport.
tldr.outcome: A device can request a location in a chosen form, but the IP address used to identify it may be misleading across some NAT or VPN arrangements. RFC 5985 is updated by RFC 7840.

today: RFC 5985 is a Proposed Standard for HELD and is updated by RFC 7840.

sections.title: A Device Requests Its Location
sections.content:
HELD is a Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol between a device and a Location Information Server (LIS), usually in the same access network. It does not define how the LIS determines the location.

The device first discovers the LIS address using a separate discovery protocol. The LIS normally identifies the device from the source IP address of its request, so address translation or a VPN can affect whether the returned location is accurate.
sections.plainLanguage: A device sends a request to a location server associated with its network. The protocol asks the server for location, but leaves the actual location-determination method to the server.

sections.title: Location by Value or by Reference
sections.content:
A device can ask the LIS to return a Presence Information Data Format Location Object (PIDF-LO), which carries location directly. It can instead request a Location URI that another authorized party can use to retrieve location information.

A location URI refers to the most current available location rather than a fixed location snapshot. The URI can be globally reachable, but possessing it does not by itself authorize access to the location.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can send the location in the reply or send a link-like URI that refers to it. A URI is a reference to location, not a promise that everyone who has it can read the location.

sections.title: Requests, Responses, and Errors
sections.content:
HELD defines three XML messages: locationRequest, locationResponse, and error. A request can name the desired location types, such as civic, geodetic, or location URI, and can include a response-time hint.

If the requested type is not exact, a LIS may return additional or alternative types. If the request requires exact types, the server must return the requested types or an error. An error includes a registered code and may include a human-readable message.
sections.plainLanguage: A request can say what kind of location the device wants. With an exact request, the server either provides that type or reports an error; otherwise, it may return an available alternative.

sections.title: Carrying HELD over HTTP
sections.content:
The RFC requires conforming devices and LISs to support HTTP and HTTP over TLS. A HELD request is sent as an HTTP POST body with the application/held+xml media type and UTF-8 XML.

Both HELD success replies and HELD application-level error messages use a successful HTTP response status. The server should prevent intermediaries from caching location responses, which could otherwise expose a location or serve stale information.
sections.plainLanguage: HELD messages travel in HTTP POST requests and responses. HTTPS can protect the exchange, and servers should prevent location replies from being cached by intermediaries.

sections.title: Protecting Location Information
sections.content:
Clients should verify that they contacted the proper LIS, and TLS must be available for bindings that support it. An integrity-protected channel prevents a response from being changed in transit; encryption helps keep location private from observers.

The LIS must verify that the requester is the target whose location it returns. Using the request's IP address as proof of identity can be vulnerable to spoofing or address reuse, so Location URIs have limited lifetimes and should be invalidated when the LIS can no longer locate the device.
sections.plainLanguage: Location should be sent only to the device it describes and protected while in transit. IP addresses can be spoofed or reused, so the server must also manage the lifetime of location references.
